title: The common language shipping still lacks
summary: The shipping industry's persistent lack of common digital standards for vessel data creates a critical accountability gap. Inconsistent definitions for emissions and operational metrics directly undermine accurate carbon intensity reporting, rendering genuine decarbonisation claims unverifiable. Without standardized, auditable data, FuelEU Maritime fines and CII ratings risk being based on opaque figures, facilitating continued greenwashing.
content:
Shipping’s digital ambitions are accelerating faster than the structures beneath them. The industry largely agrees on the need for open standards, but adoption remains constrained by proprietary interests, regulatory fragmentation and the absence of firm mandates. The latest chapter from SplashTech’s new magazine.

Shipping is no longer digitising in a regulatory vacuum, but the rules beneath its technology remain uneven, incomplete and slower moving than the tools entering daily use.

The clearest recent marker comes from the International Maritime Organization, whose Maritime Safety Committee has just adopted the International Code of Safety for Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships. The voluntary MASS Code entered into force on July 1, opening an experience-building phase before mandatory requirements are developed.

The code covers decision-support systems, remotely controlled ships, fully autonomous vessels and remote operations centres. Its weakness is scope. It says far less about the AI assistants, predictive maintenance tools and administrative software already spreading through wheelhouses, engine rooms and shore offices.

The pressure is increasing as the EU AI Act moves into full enforcement, exposing companies to penalties when they cannot explain how systems are governed, what data they use and who remains accountable for decisions shaped by automated recommendations.

That governance challenge sits above a more basic problem. Shipping still lacks a common digital language.

One language for vessel data

Asked which single standard the industry should mandate, contributors repeatedly return to vessel data. P K Mishra, managing director of IRClass, calls for common definitions covering equipment identity, sensor tags, voyage events, emissions, maintenance and noon-report equivalents.

“Shipping does not suffer from a lack of data; it suffers from inconsistent data definitions,” he tells SplashTech. The aim, he stresses, is not to centralise every record, but to define minimum structures and meanings so information can move reliably between owners, yards, manufacturers, charterers, class societies and software providers.

Patrick Ryan, senior vice-president and chief technology officer at ABS, says integration is among digitalisation’s largest hidden costs. Owners repeatedly fund bespoke work to connect systems because each vendor uses its own format and interface. With standardised data, adding a tool could become “close to plug-and-play rather than a six-month exercise”.

Pankaj Sharma, chief executive of OneLink Performance, describes interoperability as the foundation for AI, autonomy, emissions management and safer operations. Daniel Koch, head of vessel optimisation at Manta Marine Technologies, makes the commercial case: too much time is spent cleaning, preparing and integrating information before anyone can use it.

Pradeep Chawla, chief executive of MarinePals, focuses on machinery. The full benefits of automation and reliability cannot be realised, he argues, unless data produced by different equipment can be analysed together. Casper Jensen, chief executive of GTT Marine, similarly calls for standardised, high-frequency operational data that automates reporting and prevents owners being trapped inside proprietary ecosystems.

Nikhil Mathew, chairman and co-founder of Admaren Tech, widens the proposed standard to cargo particulars, tank data, hydrostatic information, port restrictions, voyage instructions and operational status. “A common standard would not force companies to use the same software,” he tells SplashTech. It would allow systems to communicate while preserving competition, provided secure authentication and responsibility for shared data are built in from the start.SUBHEAD: Enter once, use everywhere

The strongest immediate case for standardisation may be reporting. Gry Sørås, head of branding and sustainability at Siglar, selects a global format for emissions and voyage data exchange. The same information currently exists in multiple forms, increasing cost while weakening data quality precisely as environmental performance becomes a commercial issue.

Friederike Hesse, managing director of ZERO44, would begin with the noon report, the foundational input for EU ETS, FuelEU Maritime, CII, EU MRV and IMO DCS. Reports arrive in numerous proprietary formats, forcing operators, compliance platforms and verifiers to cleanse and normalise data before meaningful work begins.

Credible frameworks already exist, Hesse notes, including the Smart Maritime Council’s Standardised Vessel Dataset and Energy LEAP’s Vessel Emissions Reporting Standard. “The technical groundwork is largely done. What is missing is mandate,” she tells SplashTech. Vendors have little incentive to surrender formats that create switching costs.

Michael DeVolld, cybersecurity lead at ABS Consulting, reaches the same conclusion from the regulatory side. He calls for one harmonised emissions format across IMO DCS, EU MRV, FuelEU and national schemes: information “entered once, reused everywhere”. This would return thousands of working hours while improving the evidence received by regulators.

From chartering to port calls

Standards are also needed around commercial decisions. Christoffer Svard, chief commercial officer at Sea, wants a harmonised record of chartering communications. Negotiations and decisions are scattered across WhatsApp, email and Teams, leaving the industry dependent on inconsistent, difficult-to-reconstruct threads. A common structure would make that information usable across the value chain without forcing every participant onto one platform.

Capt Kuba Szymanski, secretary-general of InterManager, points to the continuing bureaucracy surrounding port calls. A genuinely global Maritime Single Window would allow one standardised documentation set to be accepted by every port, replacing repeated submissions and incompatible national requirements.

Other contributors identify less obvious but equally valuable common languages. Henning Davies, chief executive of LedgID, advocates a globally interoperable standard for professional identity, credentials and verification events. Qualifications and compliance records should move securely across employers and jurisdictions rather than being repeatedly collected and checked.

Ronald Spithout, managing director of OneHealth by VIKAND, extends that concept to seafarer-owned professional, personal and health records. A consent-based framework could reduce administration, improve labour mobility and give medical teams trusted information during emergencies.

Vikas Pandey, chief executive of Shipfinex, proposes a universal, real-time vessel ownership and encumbrance registry. Title, mortgages and liens are currently fragmented across flags, banks, insurers and law firms. One authoritative record would reduce fraud, accelerate transactions and make shipping assets easier for institutional capital to understand.

Craig West, chief executive Europe at Weathernews, wants a machine-readable standard for operating severity. Terms such as heavy weather remain subjective, leaving systems, operators, insurers and regulators without a shared baseline for disruption, claims or voyage decisions.

The answer is not one giant maritime database. Peter Kraehenbuehl, vice-president at WinGD, argues for structured ship-wide exchange combining common data models, cyber principles, access rights and clear responsibilities. “A ship is not a collection of isolated equipment. It is a system,” he says.

Shipping already has many of the technical ingredients it needs. What it lacks is disciplined adoption and authority. A standard only creates value when competitors use it, regulators recognise it and customers can move their information without penalty. Until that happens, AI and automation will continue to sit on fragmented foundations, and the industry will keep paying people to translate between systems that should already understand one another.

title: The IMO GHG working group – a BIMCO account
summary: The IMO's 22nd GHG working group meeting predictably concluded with persistent disagreements on crucial mid-term measures, demonstrating a continued lack of real progress. Despite previous "unanimous" declarations, member states now lack universal consensus on the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy's ambition and indicative checkpoints. While delegates talk, the industry remains largely unchecked, ensuring sustained high carbon intensity and HFO consumption for the foreseeable future.
content:
From 1-4 September 2026, the 22nd meeting of the intersessional working group on reduction of greenhouse gases from shipping took place at the IMO Headquarters in London. We were represented throughout the full week. Below is an account of the discussions, potential and hurdles following a week of intensive multilateral negotiations.

This was the first working group (WG) meeting during which new terms of reference that were agreed at MEPC 84 in the spring, were up for discussion. The terms of reference allow for both existing and new submissions to be discussed which we believe is important. The importance lies in the formal purpose of the WG which is seeking agreement on a broader text that can be acceptable to all, following the extraordinary MEPC meeting in October last year when the Net-Zero Framework (NZF) faced fierce opposition from several member states.

The four days were largely spent on deliberations on the first agenda item:

The Group is instructed, taking into account documents submitted to MEPC 84 and 85, previous sessions of ISWG-GHG, as well as documents submitted to ISWG-GHG 22 and 23, as applicable, to: 1: consider proposals, including those contained in the documents referred to above, on how to address concerns with the draft amendments to MARPOL Annex VI on the Net-Zero Framework, in line with the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy.

The overall takeaway from this meeting is that IMO member states continue to engage constructively in the discussions, but that disagreements on several crucial issues relating to a possible future IMO mid-term measure persist.

Several delegations recalled the unanimous agreement on the 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships, while many other delegations refrained from making explicit reference to the strategy.

Based on our observations, it appears that there may no longer be universal agreement on the strategy’s ambition and indicative checkpoints.

Disagreements on central parts of a future framework are of such magnitude that convergence already by December seems challenging.

Substantive issues of divergence

It was evident from statements made by member states that there is still wide disagreement on substantive parts of the framework.

That is particularly the case for the Greenhouse Gas Fuel Intensity (GFI) trajectory itself: what shape should the trajectory have? Should it be a 2-tier GFI as in the NZF or a single tier as in FuelEUMaritime?

The trajectory question is not only about setting the regulatory requirements to the reductions. It is also about whether the requirements should be set by the regulators as opportunistic requirements seeking to drive the availability of the required fuels, or whether the reduction requirements should be set based on availability, scalability and affordability of fuels in the market.

The question on one versus two tiers may be of less significance in this relation but more about the system’s ability to generate funds.

Whether funds should be generated in the framework is another issue of divergence. The NZF has a 2-tier GFI structure with the distinct ability to generate substantial amounts of funds to be channelled through a central Fund operated by the IMO. Several member states oppose this for a variety of reasons – one being the prerogative of sovereign states to levy taxes on their respective citizens.

Several other states welcome the fund-generating aspect of a framework so that just and equitable transition (JET) can be facilitated by compensating eligible states for disproportionate negative impacts (DNI).

It is our observation that this core disagreement seems to have widened substantially since the MEPC 83 approval of the NZF.

Spending funds generated by a framework

This is also an area of disagreement. Are collected funds to be spent entirely in-sector? Or is there a case for giving funds to states for their own use? Some member states firmly believe the framework should not generate funds by itself but rather leave any monetisation of elements of the framework to the private sector.

Support for zero or near-zero fuels and technologies is also an area of some divergence. Should such fuel and energy sources be rewarded in excess of surplus unit (SU) generation? Should there be a multiplier to amplify use of such fuels and technologies? Naturally, any possible reward would also need to be contingent on the stringency of the trajectory in the first place.

Does everything have to be agreed as one package? Some member states argue that a push to see everything resolved, rather than moving on to elements that enjoy agreement now, is not ideal. Other states believe that since the core architecture of the GFI is less controversial, a package of technical mid-term measures should be pushed first, after which agreement on the economic element can be sought.

The discussion on an IMO Fund or Facility is however not purely political or principal. It may have very practical implications for the industry, and the world, as it is presently the “safety-valve” which prevents ships from potentially becoming stranded assets should the over- and under-compliance not balance. A purely technical measure without the ability to either pay for compliance, or some other measure, risk resulting in some ships being rendered unable to trade.

Next step

While this session of the WG did little to forge consensus on the matters of divergence, there were sporadic signs of willingness to compromise. However, such compromise is still short of detail and more work is needed.

The WG will continue deliberations at the next meeting which takes place in the week preceding the MEPC 85 in November this year. We expect new submissions to this 23rd meeting of the WG and we expect member states to pursue bilateral agreements on core issues in the interim.

title: The efficiency formula behind Navibulgar’s fleet renewal
summary: Navibulgar details a decade-long fleet renewal with "innovative" bulk carriers, asserting enhanced efficiency and a reduced environmental footprint. Yet, the company offers no concrete data on actual carbon intensity reductions per tonne-mile, nor specifies the fuel types used across its expanded fleet. Without transparent, verifiable emissions performance beyond vague "market standards," these claims remain suspect, failing to demonstrate genuine progress against FuelEU Maritime targets.
content:
Navibulgar has spent more than a decade building a new generation of bulk carriers designed to outperform market standards.

Working with DNV, the company has combined innovative design, fuel efficiency, and operational flexibility to create one of the youngest and most efficient fleets in its segment.

When Navigation Maritime Bulgare (Navibulgar), a leading owner of bulk carriers typically operating on spot market charters, takes delivery of three 45,000 dwt Handymax bulk carriers in 2027, this will be the completion of a series comprising 16 nearly identical vessels delivered since 2016. In addition, fifteen 32,000 dwt “Lakers” have been commissioned since 2021, and the last of them, m/v Stara Planina, was successfully delivered on 20 August. And that is not the end of Navibulgar’s ambitious fleet renewal programme – a set of eight 71,000 dwt units is slated for construction over the coming years, with deliveries due to start in 2028 and continuing into 2029. The average age of the fleet stands at just 7 years, says Executive Director Aleksandar Kalchev.

Hull design optimization and lightship recalculation maximize efficiency

There is a common concept underlying the entire endeavour, which dates back to 2014: “We were looking to build vessels that are different from the market standard and would perform better than the average,” explains Kalchev. As both a naval architect and an experienced shipmaster, he has been steering the company’s fortunes since 2013, contributing his experience in both disciplines.

Seeking to benefit from innovative hull optimization technology, Navibulgar had scanned the market for a competent classification society to help develop the best designs for the programme. “We concluded that DNV offered the expertise we were looking for. The hull optimization they delivered for both vessel types has enabled us to achieve greater efficiency while lowering the environmental footprint of the vessels.”

‘’ The hull optimization DNV delivered for both vessel types has enabled us to achieve greater efficiency while lowering the environmental footprint of the vessels. ‘’

Aleksandar Kalchev Executive Director , Navibulgar

DNV also performed complex lightship recalculations to reduce excessive material thickness in certain parts of the hulls, thereby making the ships lighter than competing designs, reports Miroslav Hristov, Senior Principal Surveyor at DNV. “We succeeded in reducing the lightweight of the vessels by several hundred tonnes, increasing the deadweight, which makes them more competitive.”

Extended cubic capacity minimizes fuel consumption and emissions per tonne-mile

“All the knowledge we have built over the years has been implemented in our newbuilds,” explains Kalchev. “In addition to the optimized hull shape and low resistance, we maximized the cubic capacity by subdividing the hull into cargo holds and shaping the cargo spaces in a precisely calculated way while minimizing the engine room and the unused forward portion of the vessel.”

The resulting capacity of the new Handymaxes is actually closer to that of larger Supramaxes, he adds.

Slow-steaming strategy saves fuel

“We always try for the lowest specific fuel consumption for each voyage,” says Kalchev. “The average speed of our fleet is 11 knots; we are pretty much slow steaming all the time.” For its newbuilds, Navibulgar chose modern, electrically controlled engines that can operate at very low revolutions and are small, requiring less space, explains DNV’s Miroslav Hristov. “To ensure that they can reach optimum cruising speed faster, despite their small size, without producing excessive smoke, electric compressors were added to supply extra air to the turbochargers. DNV approved this solution, which was developed together with the engine manufacturer MAN.” With all the optimizations implemented, the vessels consume 25 to 35 per cent less fuel than the company’s older tonnage built from 2010 to 2012, confirms Kalchev.

Shallow draught and strong cranes increase flexibility

With a maximum draught of 10.5 metres, the vessels are suitable for shallow ports, Kalchev points out. “What is more, the cargo cranes are stronger, and the hatch covers larger than typical for this ship type, which makes it easier to load oversized break-bulk cargo such as long steel products. All that makes our ships more versatile, giving them an additional competitive edge.”

The first three 45,000 dwt newbuilds, delivered between 2016 and 2019, were proof that Navibulgar’s choices were spot on.

“They are showing very good fuel consumption, and their other features make them especially interesting for the Atlantic trades,” says Kalchev. Navibulgar entrusted Yangzijiang Shipbuilding Group with the remainder of its orders. The yard has since delivered 25 vessels to the owner’s full satisfaction, with 11 more on order.

Taking fleet renewal to the next level with 71,000 dwt vessels

Having identified another market niche to fill, Navibulgar recently ordered eight 71,000 dwt units. “We are seeing cargo parcels going up,” reasons Kalchev. “To accommodate them, we are building a bigger Ultramax in the 60,000-plus-ten-per-cent deadweight range, which is quite unusual. As with our previous newbuilds, we want to offer the most efficient vessels that can carry more cargo while using the same quantity of fuel, resulting in a smaller ecological footprint per tonne.”

Top CII ratings confirmed by DNV

In terms of decarbonization, Kalchev says his modern ships are performing so well that he is confident they will remain compliant going into the 2030s and ’40s. “DNV provided us with a sophisticated algorithm for the calculation of the Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) and the EU ETS,” he says. “All our vessels built since 2016 have CII ratings of A or B, most of them CII A, the highest standard. They don’t need any additional energy-efficiency devices to comply. I believe that our new fleet will be one of the most efficient in this segment worldwide.”

With slow steaming and blend-in biofuels, Navibulgar can maintain these ratings, says Kalchev. “DNV is keeping a close eye on the entire fleet’s emission performance, managing our reports and verifying them using its Emissions Connect service.

Furthermore, a designated person at DNV’s office in Poland is supporting us in implementing FuelEU Maritime, including pooling.”

A partnership focused on safety, quality, and reliability

“Quality is maybe the most important thing when you build a ship,” Kalchev states. “You must select the makers carefully because the vessel must be reliable and safe.” As an example, he points to the importance of smooth, flat welded seams on the ships’ plating for reducing resistance in water.

Looking for the right partner to carry this quality strategy into the future, Navibulgar recently entrusted its safety and quality management systems to DNV. Close contact with the head office in Oslo and guaranteed around-the-clock support from DNV were strong arguments for a closer partnership. Navibulgar is an avid user of DNV’s unique DATE service, providing any-time access to technical experts. Now the company is trialling DNV’s Steel Load Planner, which helps prepare optimized and fully safety-approved loading plans for heavy cargo such as steel coils.

How Navibulgar is preparing for its next phase of growth

“I am happy about our broad cooperation,” says Kalchev, “because the majority of our fleet is in DNV class, and it will be better with DNV having a closer eye on the office as well. DNV is a global leader in classification, with deep technical expertise and a strong track record of supporting the maritime industry. As an organization that also strives to lead in our field, we see significant value in partnering with industry leaders who share our commitment to excellence.”

title: bound4blue secures Bureau Veritas Design Assessment for Model 3-24 eSAIL®
summary: bound4blue's Model 3-24 eSAIL® suction sail system recently received a Bureau Veritas Design Assessment, aiming to bolster shipowner "confidence" in wind propulsion. Despite claims of "regulatory gains" and 13 installations, the announcement lacks specific, independently verified data on actual CO2 tonne reductions or its tangible impact on FuelEU Maritime compliance. True decarbonization requires transparent performance metrics demonstrating significant carbon intensity improvements, not just design approvals or increased unit orders, to avoid greenwashing.
content:
bound4blue has received a Design Assessment from Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore for its flagship Model 3-24 eSAIL®, developed to maximise the contribution of wind propulsion on larger vessels.

Presented during a handover ceremony at SMM 2026 in Hamburg, the assessment confirms that the design has been independently reviewed against Bureau Veritas’ technical requirements, providing further confidence for shipowners looking to deploy proven, scalable wind propulsion solutions.

Market moves

bound4blue’s eSAIL® suction sail technology has made significant strides forward across multiple shipping segments in the space of the past year, with more than 50 units now ordered and installations completed onboard 13 vessels.

The Model 3 range spans heights from 24 metres to 36 metres, with the 3-24 becoming the first commercial installation earlier this year onboard Klaveness Combination Carriers’ newbuild MV Baltazar. The sails feature an expanded surface area and optimised aerodynamic profile, ensuring even the largest ships can take advantage of compelling commercial and regulatory gains.

Confidence counts

“As the market matures, confidence becomes just as important as innovation,” says José Miguel Bermúdez, CEO and co-founder of bound4blue. “So, as wind takes its place within mainstream fleet investment, independent assessments really do play an increasingly important role in differentiating and substantiating technical solutions.

“Here at bound4blue it’s been a focus since day one. We are committed to engaging with leading Class societies to demonstrate the quality and potential of our proprietary technology. By doing so we provide owners, yards and wider industry stakeholders with the reassurance they need to embrace the wind revolution and unlock significant environmental and business benefits. We’re delighted to achieve this latest recognition from Bureau Veritas as we continue to cement our position as a trusted industry partner.”

Supporting progress

The Model 3-24 builds on bound4blue’s proven Model 2 platform, retaining the company’s hallmark technical simplicity for straightforward installation and autonomous operation.

eSAILs® work by utilising boundary layer suction to draw air across an aerodynamically optimised surface and generate propulsive force up to seven times greater than rigid sails of the same size, while requiring far less maintenance. The result is significantly lower fuel consumption, reduced CO₂ emissions and improved operational efficiency. In addition, the non-ATEX technology supports compliance with a growing range of environmental regulations, including FuelEU Maritime and the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), while contributing towards improved Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) performance and EEXI compliance.

Speaking of the Design Assessment process, David Barrow, SVP for Western Europe and Americas at Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore, comments: “Wind propulsion is becoming an increasingly important element of the maritime industry’s decarbonisation journey, and independent technical assessment helps provide confidence as these technologies continue to mature and scale. Through this Design Assessment, Bureau Veritas is pleased to support bound4blue in advancing safe and reliable innovation, helping shipowners reduce emissions while maintaining robust technical standards.”

Plug and play

eSAILs® have emerged as a solution of choice for many of shipping’s leading names, including companies such as Maersk Tankers, Eastern Pacific Shipping, Odfjell, Louis Dreyfus Company, and many more.

Designed as a simple, plug-and-play system for both retrofits and newbuilds, bound4blue suction sails operate alongside conventional propulsion systems while also supporting the adoption of future fuels such as methanol and ammonia, helping shipowners integrate complementary sustainability solutions into their decarbonisation strategies.

title: Europe’s Largest Carbon Capture Facility Opens, Sending CO2 by Ship to North Sea Storage
summary: Europe's largest carbon capture facility at Yara will now ship 800,000 tonnes of CO2 annually for North Sea storage, establishing a new cross-border maritime transport chain. This initiative, however, creates additional shipping demand, raising concerns about the carbon intensity and FuelEU Maritime compliance of these new CO2 carriers. True maritime decarbonization demands a reduction in *all* operational emissions at source, not merely the creation of new routes to haul industrial waste.
content:
Europe’s largest industrial carbon capture facility has officially opened at Yara’s ammonia and fertilizer complex in Sluiskil, the Netherlands, creating a new cross-border CO2 supply chain that will rely on specialized ships to carry captured carbon to permanent storage beneath the North Sea.

The facility can capture and liquefy up to 800,000 tons of CO2 annually from ammonia production. From Sluiskil, the liquefied CO2 will be loaded aboard Northern Lights’ purpose-built CO2 carriers and transported to the company’s receiving terminal at Øygarden on Norway’s west coast.

From there, the CO2 will travel through a roughly 100-kilometer pipeline before being injected into the Aurora reservoir about 2,600 meters beneath the North Sea seabed.

Yara said the project is expected to capture and permanently store around 12 million tons of CO2 over the next 15 years.

“This is an important day for Yara and for European industry,” said Yara International President and CEO Svein Tore Holsether. “The carbon capture facility in Sluiskil proves that large-scale industrial decarbonization is possible today.”

The inauguration was attended by Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten, European Commissioner for Climate, Net Zero and Clean Growth Wopke Hoekstra and Holsether.

The project is particularly significant because it links industrial carbon capture in the Netherlands with ship-based transport and permanent geological storage in Norway, demonstrating a commercial cross-border carbon capture and storage, or CCS, chain.

Northern Lights, a joint venture between Equinor, Shell and TotalEnergies, began commercial operations last year after successfully injecting its first CO2 into storage beneath the North Sea.

Its first cargoes came from Heidelberg Materials’ cement plant in Brevik, Norway, with CO2 transported aboard specialized vessels to the Øygarden terminal.

The first phase of Northern Lights has capacity to handle 1.5 million tons of CO2 annually and is fully booked. A second phase, approved in 2025, is expected to increase capacity to at least 5 million tons per year. The expansion has received €131 million in support from the European Union’s Connecting Europe Facility for Energy program.

Yara’s Sluiskil volumes will add another major industrial source to the network and help establish seaborne CO2 transportation as an increasingly important part of Europe’s emerging carbon-management infrastructure.

“This is a milestone we have been looking forward to,” said Tim Heijn, managing director of Northern Lights. “Together, we are demonstrating that capture and cross-border CO2 transport and storage is a viable solution for European industry.”

The development also highlights a potentially significant new shipping market. Large-scale CCS projects increasingly depend on liquefied CO2 carriers to connect industrial emitters that cannot economically access storage sites by pipeline.

Northern Lights has developed purpose-built ships for that role, transporting liquefied CO2 at low temperature and elevated pressure between European industrial sites and Norway.

At Sluiskil, Yara will capture CO2 generated during ammonia production, liquefy it and hold it in storage tanks until collection by Northern Lights vessels. Capturing the emissions will also allow Yara to avoid European carbon costs associated with the volumes sent for permanent storage.

Yara operates what it describes as Europe’s largest ammonia and fertilizer plant at Sluiskil. The company said CCS will help reduce the carbon footprint of products including fertilizers and ammonia, with potential applications extending to low-carbon fuels for shipping.

European policymakers increasingly see CCS as one of the tools needed to decarbonize industries where eliminating emissions through electrification or renewable energy alone remains difficult, including fertilizer, cement and waste management.

“Europe needs practical climate solutions that deliver real emissions reductions while strengthening industrial competitiveness,” Hoekstra said. “The carbon capture and storage project at Sluiskil shows what is possible when innovation and cross-border cooperation come together.”

For Northern Lights, the Yara project also marks another step toward transforming CO2 transport and storage from a demonstration project into a broader commercial service serving industrial customers across Europe.

Equinor, which provides technical services for Northern Lights, has said it is targeting development of between 30 million and 50 million tons per year of CO2 transport and storage capacity by 2035 across projects in Europe and the United States.

With Yara’s Sluiskil facility now entering the chain, specialized CO2 shipping is moving from an emerging concept toward an operational component of Europe’s industrial decarbonization infrastructure.

title: UK shipping launches alternative fuels coalition
summary: A new UK coalition, spearheaded by the UK Chamber of Shipping and CLIA, promises to accelerate alternative maritime fuels and infrastructure. While this initiative gathers industry players to discuss future fuel availability, it presents no immediate mandate for UK vessels to reduce their current excessive HFO consumption. Such coalitions often delay tangible action; dirtiestships.com demands immediate, verifiable cuts in actual carbon intensity, not just future fuel discussions.
content:
The UK Chamber of Shipping and Cruise Lines International Association have launched a new coalition aimed at accelerating access to alternative maritime fuels and the infrastructure needed to support them.

The UK Alternative Maritime Fuels Coalition brings together shipowners, fuel suppliers, producers and maritime technology developers as the country looks to move its domestic shipping sector towards net zero.

Members include the International Bunkering Industry Association, SEA-LNG, Hydrogen UK, the Global Methanol Alliance, UK Ammonia Alliance, eFuel Alliance and groups representing carbon capture, renewable fuels and bioresources.

The coalition will focus on one of shipping’s biggest decarbonisation bottlenecks: ensuring cleaner fuels are available at scale, backed by port infrastructure and a policy framework capable of attracting investment.

It will also provide input into the UK government’s forthcoming consultation on domestic maritime fuel regulation and push for a technology-neutral approach covering fuel production, certification, port readiness and onboard systems.

A key demand will be for revenues raised from the inclusion of maritime in the UK Emissions Trading Scheme to be recycled into shipping decarbonisation.

“Access to alternative fuels is one of the defining challenges for the future of UK shipping,” said UK Chamber of Shipping chief executive Rhett Hatcher.

CLIA UK and Ireland executive director Andy Harmer said the transition depends on fuels being available “at scale, in the places ships need them”.

The coalition will meet regularly, with the UK Chamber of Shipping and CLIA acting as joint facilitators.

title: Maritime nations warn wars, shadow fleets are eroding global shipping rules
summary: The Consultative Shipping Group's alarm over eroding maritime rules and the rise of "shadow fleets" directly threatens environmental accountability in shipping. These unregulated vessels, operating outside conventional oversight, present a significant risk for unchecked emissions and excessive HFO consumption. Without transparent data and adherence to international standards, these fleets will continue to undermine efforts to achieve global decarbonization targets and avoid FuelEU Maritime fines.
content:
Eighteen of the world’s major maritime nations have warned that the international rules underpinning commercial shipping are beginning to break down, as wars, attacks on vessels and the growth of opaque shadow fleets change the environment in which more than 80% of global trade moves.

Wars, attacks on vessels and the growth of opaque shadow fleets are changing the environment in which more than 80% of global trade moves.

The warning came from the Consultative Shipping Group, or CSG, an alliance of maritime authorities from Europe, Asia and North America. Its members collectively represent about a fifth of global shipping tonnage.

The group said the battle over the Strait of Hormuz, sanctions and the expansion of vessels operating outside conventional insurance and regulatory systems should not be treated as isolated crises.

They were not “episodic shocks” but “signals of a structural shift” in the operating environment for world trade, the CSG said.

The CSG was created to defend open access to international shipping markets. Its 18 members are Belgium, Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Japan, South Korea, the Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Singapore, Spain, Sweden and the UK.

Denmark holds the chairmanship and secretariat.

The Danish Maritime Authority describes the group’s core purpose as protecting “open and unimpeded access” to shipping markets. It also seeks to counter discriminatory or restrictive maritime measures.

In September 2025, the CSG called for the preservation of a rules-based maritime order and warned against protectionism and regionalization.

That concern has since become considerably less theoretical.

Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has fallen sharply amid fighting involving Iran and the US. Only seven commodity vessels were recorded crossing the strait on Monday, according to Kpler data cited by Reuters.

Before the war, daily traffic was many times higher.

Some vessels may be travelling with tracking systems disabled, meaning the observed count could understate actual movements.

The 10-day average recently fell to about 10 commodity ships a day, its lowest since May. The decline came after attacks involving US and Iranian forces spilled directly into commercial shipping.

The deterioration challenges a basic assumption that has underpinned international commerce for decades. Commercial ships have generally been able to pass through international sea lanes regardless of political disputes between surrounding countries.

International Maritime Organization rules cover ship safety, security, construction, operations and environmental standards.

The UN agency says a safe and predictable global regulatory framework is essential because international shipping carries more than 80% of global trade.

Shadow fleet creates parallel shipping system

The second concern is the rapid expansion of the so-called shadow fleet. These are largely older tankers used to transport oil affected by sanctions on countries including Russia and Iran.

Such vessels often have opaque ownership and may change flags or identities. They can operate with limited scrutiny and, in some cases, rely on insurance outside the established Western protection and indemnity system.

Industry estimates cited by the Financial Times put the shadow tanker fleet at more than 1,500 vessels.

Reuters has separately reported that hundreds of such ships are transporting sanctioned Iranian and Russian oil with limited insurance, safety checks or regulatory scrutiny.

The problem goes beyond sanctions enforcement. Part of the global fleet operates under established insurance, environmental, transparency and safety standards. Another part increasingly operates outside them.

The result is effectively a two-tier maritime system.

The CSG says the answer is not simply to write more rules. It wants existing international rules enforced more consistently across jurisdictions and governments to cooperate more closely on free navigation and fair competition.

The stakes extend well beyond shipowners.

UN Trade and Development says maritime transport carries more than 80% of goods traded worldwide by volume. It connects raw-material suppliers, factories and consumer markets. Disruption at major sea lanes can quickly feed into freight costs, energy prices, food supplies and manufacturing chains.

Recent crises at the Suez Canal, Panama Canal, Red Sea and Strait of Hormuz have shown how disruptions at narrow maritime chokepoints can force ships onto longer routes and raise transport costs.

title: IMO weighs softer 2030 emissions target to revive Net Zero Framework
summary: The IMO is reportedly softening its 2030 greenhouse gas fuel intensity (GFI) reduction targets, a politically motivated move to revive its stalled Net Zero Framework that directly undermines early decarbonization. Original proposals for a stringent 21% GFI reduction by 2030 are being diluted, reducing pressure on shipowners to invest in cleaner fuels and prolonging reliance on high-carbon options. This compromise offers polluters a reprieve, hindering critical early demand for vital green hydrogen-derived fuels like ammonia and e-methanol and delaying genuine climate action.
content:
A potential compromise to weaken the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) emissions requirements around 2030 could reduce early demand for hydrogen-derived fuels, as governments seek to revive the regulator’s stalled Net Zero Framework (NZF).

IMO member states discussed adjusting the framework’s greenhouse gas fuel intensity (GFI) trajectory during negotiations in London from 1 to 4 September, with an emerging landing zone understood to involve less stringent requirements around 2030.

Under the original IMO proposal, ships would have been required to progressively reduce the lifecycle greenhouse gas intensity (GFI) of the energy they use, compared with a reference value of 93.3gCO2e/MJ.

By 2030, the framework set a base GFI reduction target of 8% and a more stringent “direct compliance” target of 21%. Ships failing to meet the targets would face compliance costs, while those outperforming the stricter threshold could generate surplus compliance units.

It was upended in 2025 after a coalition of member states voted against the carbon pricing elements of the framework. Now nations are mulling a less stringent 2030 target before ramping up ambition toward 2040.

Such a compromise could make the framework more politically acceptable, but would also reduce the pressure on shipowners to decarbonise during the early years of the regulation.

That could have implications for proposed green hydrogen projects targeting the maritime sector, particularly producers of green ammonia and e-methanol seeking long-term offtake agreements with shipowners.

Many such projects are targeting start-up around the end of this decade or the early 2030s, meaning a weaker initial GFI trajectory could coincide with the period in which developers need new sources of demand to underpin investment decisions.

However, a softer trajectory could ultimately prove more valuable for developers if it allows IMO members to agree to the adoption of the NZF after it was postponed last year.

Financial rewards for ships using zero- or near-zero-emission fuels also appear likely to remain part of the framework, potentially offsetting some of the impact of weaker near-term GFI requirements on hydrogen-derived fuels.

The precise shape of any revised trajectory has yet to be agreed. Governments have been asked to develop compromise proposals ahead of the next round of IMO negotiations in November, immediately before the Marine Environment Protection Committee meets to consider the framework.

title: IMO carbon price heads for December showdown
summary: The IMO's proposed global carbon price is progressing, yet analysts warn the initial fuel intensity reduction pathway could soften until 2030, significantly delaying meaningful emission cuts. While projected to generate $10-15 billion annually for "just transition" and "early adoption," critical compliance and reward mechanisms remain undefined, inviting potential greenwashing. The December showdown must deliver robust, unambiguous targets to genuinely drive down carbon intensity, not merely establish another system for continued high-emitting operations.
content:
Shipping’s proposed global carbon price has survived another bruising week at the International Maritime Organization, with a clear majority of countries continuing to back the core architecture of the Net-Zero Framework ahead of a decisive round of talks in December.

Nearly 1,200 delegates participated in last week’s ISWG-GHG 22 meeting in London, where governments attempted to bridge divisions that derailed formal adoption of the framework last year.

Thirty-eight countries speaking during the session explicitly supported carbon pricing and associated revenues, compared with 17, predominantly oil-producing states, opposing the mechanism.

The framework could generate an estimated $10bn-$15bn annually, with revenues intended to reward early adoption of zero- and near-zero-emission fuels and support a just transition, particularly in developing countries.

However, plenty remains unresolved. UCL analysis suggested the initial global fuel intensity reduction pathway could be softened around 2030 before becoming considerably steeper towards 2040. Proposals covering rewards, surplus-unit trading and compliance mechanisms also remain under negotiation.

Japan’s proposal to replace centralised GHG pricing with shipowner-directed contributions gained little traction, while China’s suggestion that compliance payments and rewards could be netted into a single transaction attracted broader support.

“The devil is still in the detail,” UCL’s Shipping and Oceans Research Group cautioned, noting that several important elements remained wide open despite a more cooperative atmosphere.

Jesse Fahnestock, director of decarbonisation at the Global Maritime Forum, said member states had shown “a continued willingness to find common ground”, but warned that ambition must remain sufficient to underpin long-term investment in zero-emission shipping.

Negotiators now face an extremely compressed timetable. The next technical working group meets from November 23 to 27, immediately followed by MEPC 85 from November 30 to December 3. The extraordinary MEPC session that was adjourned last year is scheduled to resume on December 4.

The Net-Zero Framework was agreed in principle in April 2025, only for its adoption to be delayed following intense US and Saudi opposition.

title: Shipping: The EU ETS and the Energy Complex
summary: The EU ETS continues to impose escalating costs on shipping, with carbon allowances now averaging €83.30/tonne, driven by volatile gas prices and increased demand for carbon-intensive power generation. This market dynamic, where higher gas prices make coal more competitive, highlights a systemic failure to rapidly transition away from fossil fuels, impacting shipping's operational expenditures directly. Despite these rising financial pressures, the industry's actual decarbonization efforts, especially among the dirtiest vessels, remain woefully inadequate to meet urgent environmental targets.
content:
The EU ETS is expected to keep impacting shipping both in the near and in the long term, following the latest gas price increases.

In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Intermodal said that “the EUA market maintained its upward trend in August, despite the quieter trading conditions and lower liquidity that typically characterize the holiday period. The advance extended the recovery that began in late March and left the EU ETS on a constructive footing heading into autumn. The Front Dec-26 EUA contract averaged €82.36 /ton during August and at the time of writing read €83.30 /ton, around 6.5% above the 2026 y-t-d average. Prices remained within a relatively narrow range during the month, and the contract continued to trade above its 50-, 100- and 200-day moving averages. The European gas market has contributed to the firming of EUAs. Prices at the Dutch TTF hub rose significantly as geopolitical tensions leading to Qatari volumes off market, low European storage levels and competition from Asian buyers for LNG cargoes heightened concerns over winter supply”.

According to Intermodal’s Senior Analyst, Mr. Nikos Tagoulis, “although the correlation between front-month TTF gas prices and EUAs fluctuated in August, it has strengthened recently, suggesting that prevailing gas-market dynamics are supporting EUA demand. The principal transmission channel is fuel-switching economics: higher gas prices make coal more competitive with gas for power generation, encouraging more carbon-intensive output and increasing utilities’ demand for allowances. Furthermore, recent economic signals add to this supportive backdrop, pointing to firm industrial demand. The August eurozone manufacturing PMI reached its strongest level in more than four years, accompanied by stronger new orders, a recovery in exports and the first increase in factory employment after more than three years. Together, these developments strengthen the outlook for EUA demand”.

The shipbroker added that “despite the positive backdrop, traders remain cautious. Investment funds have reduced their net-long exposure in recent weeks, while commercial participants have continued to increase their forward exposure, reflecting hedging strategies built around expectations of further EUA price increases. The divergence indicates that commercial buying remains driven by risk management even as speculative interest weakens. Compliance buying adds another source of demand ahead of September 30, including from shipping companies as the maritime sector’s obligations continue to phase in. In 2026, shipping companies must surrender allowances covering 70% of their verified 2025 emissions within the scope of the EU ETS, rising to 100% of 2026 emissions in the following year, with higher EUA prices increasing the compliance cost of voyages covered by the scheme”.

“Looking ahead, policy is re-emerging as a major driver. The Commission’s July proposal for the post-2030 EU ETS would slow the contraction of the emissions cap, extend conditional free allocation and ease the operation of the Market Stability Reserve. The measures would leave more allowances in circulation than under the present framework, easing concerns about future supply constraints. The initial market response was positive, however, this is only the starting point for further negotiations, leaving scope for revision”, Mr. Tagoulis said.

He also noted that “beyond the EU ETS reform, the proposed linkage with the UK ETS remains an open issue. A summit expected to advance negotiations in July was postponed following the change in UK leadership, leaving the timetable uncertain. Progress towards linkage should narrow the spread between UKAs and EUAs as UK allowance prices move closer to EU levels. Once implemented, the linkage could become a bearish factor for EUA prices by expanding the pool of available allowances, although its impact would depend on supply conditions across both systems”.

title: IMO makes steady progress on the Net Zero Framework, with large majority continuing to back GHG pricing and centralised fund to support shipping’s transition
summary: The IMO's latest GHG working group reported majority support for a centralized carbon price (RU price), yet this "progress" remains mired in theoretical discussions. Fossil fuel-aligned states continue to hinder a concrete mechanism, ensuring the "Net Zero Framework" is far from delivering actual emission cuts. While talks persist, the world's dirtiest ships continue burning excessive HFO, contributing millions of tonnes of CO2 without immediate accountability or FuelEU Maritime-style fines.
content:
The IMO’s 22nd Intersessional Working Group on GHG emissions has concluded with significant majority of member states (two thirds of those who took the floor) supporting a centralised system for collecting revenues, operationalized through a GHG price (RU price), and disbursing it for rewards for early adopters and supporting a just and equitable transition. The group of member states focused on a technical-only solution and abandonment of GHG pricing, remained small and consistently composed of strongly fossil fuel aligned governments.

Just as at MEPC 84, the political dynamics observed at MEPC.ES2 did not occur in this meeting. The discussions were more representative of the ISWG-GHG 19 and MEPC 83 negotiating dynamics, but this does not rule out the potential for the dynamics that occurred at MEPC.ES2 returning in future meetings. That said, there was reassuring evidence from the week that reduces that risk, including in the contrast between strong public (press) positions taken against the IMO’s NZF, and the substance of how delegations negotiated in the meeting.

Dr Tristan Smith, Professor of Energy and Transport at UCL Shipping and Oceans Research Group said: “whilst there are many positives to take away – there is clear potential for a return to a strong policy solution and decision making this December, there remains high uncertainty in the extent that both industry’s transition and low-income countries’ transitions will be supported. There remains high risk that in the effort to find a creative way forwards, the equilibrium between these two aspects, that enabled the NZF in the first place, is lost to the detriment of the outcome overall.”

In addition to the discussion on centralised system for revenue collection and disbursement, the meeting discussed a number of other items as guided by the chair, discussed in detail with member state positions in the readout. Some of these included:

• GFI (Global Fuel Intensity) reduction pathway: GFI is likely to be softened initially (around 2030), but then steeper in the period to 2040.

• ZNZ rewards: ZNZ reward still broadly supported and a priority to many member states, but the broad support for a multiplier, despite it being taken off the table at the last meeting, could yet lead this to be incorporated to provide incentivisation.

• Compliance approaches:

o Most interventions confirmed support for the compliance mechanisms as setup in NZF ‘as is’. The strongest support was for the two least controversial options common to all proposals: reducing GHG intensity and pooling/transfer of SU.

o Direct contributions: Japan’s proposal to replace GHG pricing with shipowner-directed contributions was robustly rejected, particularly by the member states that would need to ‘swing’ to support it for this to start to build momentum.

o SU (Surplus Units) trading: Majority of member states opposed the inclusion of energy efficiency SU credits and the concept of printing SU’s to manage an SU price shock, citing various reasons, primarily a concern that this would destabilise the SU market and undermine investment predictability.

o Netting: China’s proposal to balance of RU and reward payments that could be netted to form a single transaction received broad support. However, the details of the concept will now need to be set out in guidelines and there remain a number of issues regarding this approach, as raised by several delegations.

Dr Annika Frosch, Research Fellow at UCL Shipping and Oceans Research Group said: “Despite the intense debate over its design, a clear majority of delegations still regard a Fund, Facility, or similar financial structure as essential to implementing the 2023 IMO Strategy. Their message is clear: without predictable financing, there can be no credible Just and Equitable Transition.”

Given all the above points, NZF ‘as is’ still remains the obvious answer (and most supported way forwards), but the process to realise that conclusion formally makes this a difficult political solution. The process from here could therefore be as much about producing what appears to be a new package, but one that broadly ends up with similar outcomes in relation to objectives.

But perhaps the most delicate part of a ‘deal’ and one that remains unclear, is the extent that a deal will support JET – at least as well as NZF ‘as is’. If support to JET does reduce, then many low-income countries currently willing to see clear mitigation stringency and obligation, could change position in support of weaker more ambiguous details, that then adds risk and cost to the transition’s investment. For now, those making investment decisions and strategy, the conclusions can be broadly stated as:

1. Do not try to use this meeting as a signal you can finalise decisions around, several key aspects of the negotiation are wide-open and didn’t narrow this week, there could well be twists to come as different concepts are merged together to find common ground. The devil is still in the detail.

2. Do still expect a clarification/agreement at MEPC 85 later this year – the spirit of cooperation was good, and the risk of a disruption equivalent to MEPC.ES2 looks lower. The chair summarised saying he was confident that the group would deliver a conclusion to its work at MEPC 85.

3. The Revised Strategy, net-zero 2050 remain reiterated touchstones by all, perhaps with different levels of sincerity/disingenuity, but will set the frame – ultimately shipping will have to decarbonise to zero in a very short time-scale. The core question is just how soft the start to the transition is, and what regulatory tools/support businesses will have to manage the risks that the detail creates of being strongly incentivised to short-term dead-ends (like LNG) before the strong regulatory incentive to move to ZNZ occurs.

Alasdair Wishart, Institute of Marine Engineering, Science and Technology (IMarEST) Technical and Policy Director said: “The maritime energy transition will be shaped by the decisions the IMO Member States make over the coming months. As the professional body representing the technical voice of maritime professionals worldwide, the IMarEST is proud to support Member States in navigating these complex choices. UCL’s modelling, building on DNV’s comprehensive impact assessment, provides a valuable framework for comparing options and understanding their real-world implications. Evidence-led analysis is essential to developing an effective Net Zero Framework and supporting delivery of the IMO’s 2023 GHG Strategy through a just and equitable transition.”

title: Shipping companies are putting sails back on cargo ships
summary: Maersk's plan to equip a container vessel with a spinning rotor sail by 2027 is a minimal step, with manufacturer Anemoi claiming merely a 10% fuel reduction. This minor efficiency gain does little to curb the hundreds of millions of tonnes of CO2 global shipping emits annually, especially when only around 100 of tens of thousands of vessels use any form of wind assist. Such "greenwashing" attempts fall short of the drastic decarbonization required to avoid significant FuelEU Maritime fines and genuinely reduce carbon intensity.
content:
Transcript

JOEL ROSE, HOST:

One of the world's largest shipping lines will soon be the first to equip a container vessel with a sail. This week, global logistics firm Maersk said it would fit the device on a cargo ship in 2027. It comes during a sea change for shipping and planet-warming pollution, as NPR's Henry Larson reports.

HENRY LARSON, BYLINE: Unlike the tall ships of old, shipping liners have no rigging for the wind to sing through.

(SOUNDBITE OF ROTOR SAIL SPINNING)

LARSON: Instead, the sail soon to be mounted on a Maersk vessel is more like a giant steel column. It's called a rotor sail.

(SOUNDBITE OF ROTOR SAIL SPINNING)

LARSON: The column uses an electric motor to spin really fast, like in this video from its manufacturer, Anemoi. And as the wind swirls around the rotating column, the pressure gives the vessel an extra boost.

CLARE URMSTON: This thrust can be used to either increase the vessel's speed or you can reduce the consumption of the main engine.

LARSON: That's Clare Urmston, CEO of Anemoi. The company markets their rotor sales as a way to save on fuel and reduce greenhouse gas emissions that are the primary driver of climate change. She says the sales have netted about a 10% reduction in fuel usage on average. But the global shipping industry contributes about 3% of the world's emissions, which comes out to hundreds of millions of tons a year.

URMSTON: The market is huge, but the market is just now starting to move from accepting the technology to actually thinking about scaling the technology.

LARSON: Right now, just over a hundred large vessels have some wind assist installed compared to the tens of thousands of large ships under the jurisdiction of the International Maritime Organization, which is the U.N. agency that regulates much of the world's shipping.

INGRID IRIGOYEN: Every single one of us can just look around your house right now and go every single thing pretty much came on a ship. So it's a huge scale. And the challenges - we've got a big mountain to climb.

LARSON: Ingrid Irigoyen is managing director of the Center for Green Market Activation. She's worked for years to get ship owners and the companies that charter them to embrace green fuels - power centers that would greatly limit the carbon emission from ships. She says things are tricky right now.

IRIGOYEN: The last 18 months or so have been pretty rocky for a lot of companies that I think had really strong, good intentions about decarbonizing their supply chains, decarbonizing their operations.

LARSON: Some shipping executives have joined a wider retreat from climate efforts this decade. Data from the International Chamber of Shipping shows many are less confident about hydrogen and ammonia and other new green products becoming commercially viable fuel sources.

GAVIN ALLWRIGHT: The cost of alternative fuels currently is very high.

LARSON: Gavin Allwright is head of a trade group that represents ship owners and companies operating wind technology.

ALLWRIGHT: So therefore, you've got to try to level that playing field for those new fuels. The interesting thing is, with wind propulsion, the higher price of the fuel, the better the business model is.

LARSON: He spoke with NPR from an international maritime organization meeting where members were debating future greenhouse gas regulations on shipping that could drastically alter the fate of green technology in the sector.

ALLWRIGHT: Whatever happens here, the industry is still moving forward. We've still got a strategy in place. We just don't have the tools in place to implement that.

LARSON: The Trump administration, along with several other countries, has worked to fracture support for what it calls a carbon tax. But the working group is still trying for a solution, one that International Chamber of Shipping's Chris Waddington says is needed.

CHRIS WADDINGTON: We need certainty - regulatory certainty - to be able to invest.

LARSON: The International Maritime Organization has more meetings this fall to try and decide the fate of a global standard for greener shipping. But in the meantime, the number of vessels sailing cleaner is slowly - very slowly - growing. Henry Larson, NPR News.
